title: How to Decide Whether to Delay Social Security to Age 70
description: Analyzing the 'Break-Even' point and longevity insurance.
content:
Social Security offers a unique deal: for every year you delay claiming between age 62 and 70, your guaranteed, inflation-adjusted income rises by roughly 8%. If you claim at 62, you get 70% of your benefit. If you claim at 70, you get 124%. Most people claim early to 'get what's theirs,' but mathematically, delaying is often the superior choice for those in good health. This guide helps you weigh the 'Bird in Hand' vs. the 'Two in the Bush'.

Key Takeaways

  • The 8% Guarantee: There is no other investment that guarantees an 8% inflation-adjusted risk-free return. Delaying Social Security is like buying the world's best annuity.
  • The Survivor Benefit: If you are the higher earner, delaying helps your spouse. If you die, they inherit your higher monthly check. Delaying is a form of life insurance.
  • The Break-Even Point: Usually around age 81. If you live past 81, delaying to 70 pays out more total lifetime dollars. Since life expectancy for a 65-year-old couple is nearly 90, the odds favor delaying.
  • The 'Bridge' Strategy: Spend down your 401(k) from age 62 to 70 to fund your life, allowing the Social Security check to grow. This lowers RMDs later and maximizes guaranteed income.

Why It Matters (US Context)

Social Security benefits are tax-advantaged in many states. Also, on the federal level, only up to 85% is taxable. Replacing fully taxable 401(k) withdrawals with partially tax-free Social Security income is a tax efficiency win.

The Dollar Difference

Scenario: Your Full Retirement Age benefit (Age 67) is $2,000/mo.

Claim at 62 (Early)

Benefit: $1,400/mo (30% cut).
Annual: $16,800.
Lifetime (to 90): $571,200.

Claim at 70 (Late)

Benefit: $2,480/mo (24% boost).
Annual: $29,760.
Lifetime (to 90): $714,240.
Difference: You get $143,000 more by waiting.

The Inflation Factor

COLA (Cost of Living Adjustments) compound better on the larger number. A 3% raise on $2,480 is bigger than a 3% raise on $1,400. The gap widens every year.

When to Claim Early (62)

  1. Poor Health: If you have a diagnosis that limits life expectancy to <75, claim immediately.
  2. Cash Crunch: If you have no savings and can't work, claim it. Survival today beats optimization tomorrow.
  3. The 'Lower Earner': In a couple, the lower earner often claims early (62) to provide cash flow, while the higher earner waits to 70 to maximize the survivor benefit. This is the 'Split Strategy'.
  4. Dependent Children: If you have minor children (e.g., you are 62 and have a 16-year-old), they can get benefits on your record. This 'Family Max' might make claiming early worth it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What if Social Security runs out?

It won't go to $0. Worst case (2033 projection), benefits are cut by ~20%. Even with a cut, the math of delaying usually holds up.

Can I invest the early checks?

You can, but can you beat the risk-free 8% growth the government offers? Probably not without risk. Taking the sure thing is usually better.

Can I change my mind?

You have one 'Do-Over' within 12 months of claiming (you must repay benefits). After Full Retirement Age, you can 'Suspend' benefits to restart the growth.
